questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presented with left arm pain and swelling for several hours. She was an active intravenous drug user. On examination, there was minimal erythema in the left antecubital fossa and upper arm with significant pain on palpation. Investigations: CT left arm: gas seen in fascial planes, suspicious for a necrotizing soft tissue infection
questions.lead_in: In addition to emergency surgical debridement, what would be the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Piperacillin–tazobactam, vancomycin, clindamycin Necrotizing soft tissue infection calls for empiric antibiotic coverage of Gram-positive (including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, MRSA), gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria. Clindamycin is added to inhibit toxin production. Piperacillin–tazobactam, vancomycin, clindamycin provides the most appropriate coverage, including that of MRSA.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q25

questions.question: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia presents with fever, hypotension, and swelling of the right thigh, with discolouration, bullae formation, and crepitus. Aspirate is performed. Presented with a gram stain.

parts.text: What type of organism is shown in the gram stain?
What is the most likely organism?

questions.model_answer: a) Organism type on Gram stain: large gram-positive bacillus (rod). b) Most likely organism: Clostridium septicum - spontaneous (non-traumatic) gas gangrene/myonecrosis in patients with hematologic malignancy and neutropenia is classically caused by C. septicum, often associated with underlying GI mucosal breakdown (e.g. neutropenic colitis/typhlitis) allowing bacteremic seeding of muscle.

parts.text: One clinical and gram stain characteristic suggestive of infection?

cohort_answer.text: C. perfringens (most common), C. septicum, C. sordellii, C. novyi. Clinical: gas in subcutaneous tissue, pain out of proportion, SIRS, dish water fluid. Gram stain: large GPB (boxcar shaped = C. perfringens; terminal spores/drumstick = C. septicum), minimal PMNs due to lethal alpha toxin. Settings: trauma injury (C. perfringens), colon adenocarcinoma/neutropenia (C. septicum); accidental traumatic injuries, war wounds, surgical wounds (bowel/biliary/septic abortion), arterial insufficiency. Management: urgent surgical debridement; empiric PipTazo/Vanco/clinda, once Clostridium confirmed Pen 24mU/day IV + Clindamycin 600mg IV q6h. Virulence factor: Alpha toxin (lecithinase damaging cell membranes, causes hemolytic anemia/thrombosis/myonecrosis/hypotension); Theta toxin (perfringolysin O) decreases microvascular perfusion and causes DIC

questions.question: A woman has a history of intermittent bloody diarrhea for the last month. She comes in with hypotension and new hemorrhagic bullae to her lower extremities. A sample is taken, with the gram stain appearing as follows (photo of Gram Positive rods with subterminal spores, no other cells visible on stain):

parts.text: a) What are two characteristics features on Gram stain?
c) What is one risk factor for this condition?
d) What is the recommended antimicrobial treatment?
e) What are two other interventions you might consider?

cohort_answer.text: Gram stain: Gram positive bacilli, subterminal spores. Organism: Clostridium septicum (if no trauma; C. perfringens if trauma). Risk factor: spontaneous gas gangrene with diarrhea history suggests GI entry, possible undiagnosed adenocarcinoma of colon; also congenital neutropenia or prior radiation to abdomen. Treatment: Penicillin 3-4 million U IV q4h + Clindamycin 600-900mg IV q8h (alternatives imipenem, meropenem or vancomycin). Other interventions: debridement/surgical intervention, hyperbaric oxygen as adjuvant.
